lead: These questions concern this loop diagram. The sections are counting units, not measured yarn lengths.

questions.title: Did pulling use up the colors?
questions.prompt: Pull one row, then knit it back. Compare the picture rather than choosing a new motif.
questions.answer: The same 192 color entries stay on the strand. Pulling changes how many sections remain in cloth; knitting returns those sections in their original order. Choosing a new picture is a different action and replaces the color plan. Nothing here simulates yarn stretching or a change in physical length.

questions.title: Why does the next row run the other way?
questions.prompt: In Dye your own, move focus across the top row and read the stitch's strand section. Then move down to the next row without dyeing.
questions.answer: The strand crosses alternate physical rows in opposite directions. In this diagram the top-left section is 192 and is released first from full cloth. The top-right section is 181, released twelfth; the next row's leftmost section is 169, released twenty-fourth. The row and column name a place, while the strand number names an order. Arrow keys only explore the grid.

questions.title: Can Undo dye put the cloth back?
questions.prompt: Dye one stitch, pull one row, and inspect Undo dye before knitting back.
questions.answer: No. Dye history remembers pictures, not the amount of yarn released. Undo dye is unavailable while any sections are loose. Knit back first; then Undo restores the earlier color plan without changing how much is knitted. Choosing a motif starts a new dye history instead of adding another remembered edit.
